data.content:
## The BIP143 preimage - what each field solves

Legacy signing hashed a modified copy of the whole transaction, once per input: that is the quadratic bomb. BIP143 replaces it with ten fields:

```
version       02000000
hashPrevouts  SHA256d(all outpoints)        ← computed once
hashSequence  SHA256d(all nSequence)        ← computed once
outpoint      txid + vout of THIS input
scriptCode    19 76a914 <pubKeyHash> 88ac
amount        spent value, LE-8
nSequence     this input's
hashOutputs   SHA256d(all outputs)          ← computed once
locktime      00000000
sighash type  01000000
```

**The three hash fields** are the fix. Everything that grows with the transaction (inputs, outputs) enters as a 32-byte fingerprint instead of a full list, so this P2WPKH preimage stays 182 bytes no matter how large the transaction grows (only P2WSH's scriptCode varies in size) - and the fingerprints are identical for every input, so a validator computes them once and reuses them. O(n²) becomes O(n). On this canvas they are the three Builder → SHA-256d pairs.

**outpoint** - the coin being authorized, stated raw. hashPrevouts pins which inputs ride together; this field pins which one *this* signature approves. Without it, two inputs locked to the same key would share an identical preimage, and one signature would unlock both.

**scriptCode** - the contract the signature commits to, same role as in legacy signing. P2WPKH has a quirk: the on-chain script is `0014<hash>`, but the scriptCode is the *implied P2PKH template* `76a914 <hash> 88ac`, because the witness program contains no CHECKSIG itself - validation runs "as if" P2PKH. The SCRIPTCODE Builder assembles exactly that.

**amount** - new in BIP143: the signature now commits to the value being spent. An offline or hardware signer no longer needs full previous transactions to know what it is signing, and a lying host can't spoof the fee.

version, nSequence, locktime, sighash type: same commitments as legacy, unchanged.
